strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: jointly choosing intervention variables and contextual information. The analytical example clearly demonstrates why intervening on every controllable variable, or ignoring context, can exclude the optimal policy.

Selecting scopes through historical averages of UCB values is a useful algorithmic idea. The decomposition into scope-selection regret and within-scope action regret provides an informative analytical framework.

The experiments use 110 seeds and 700 interventions, report uncertainty, and share the HEBO backend across the main comparisons. Context, backend, and noise ablations provide additional evidence, and the paper acknowledges a setting where CoBO converges faster.
weaknesses: The reduction from general mixed policies to contextual BO is insufficiently justified. Definition 1 permits sequential scopes such as {(X1; empty), (X2; C)} with X1 → C → X2, where intervening on X1 changes the context distribution. Sections 3 and B.1 instead assume fixed context distributions and observe context before selecting the entire action vector. Grouping scopes by their unions of action and context variables also discards the individual conditioning restrictions. Consequently, the guarantees are not established for the full causal policy class introduced in the paper.

The main regret proof contains substantive gaps. On page 27, it bounds f_i*(c) − f_i(x,c) by the range of f_i* across contexts. This is false: an action-dependent function can have a constant contextual maximum while suboptimal actions incur positive loss. Separately, the instance-dependent proof concludes with c(T), defined using worst-arm information gain gamma(T), whereas Equation (4) uses arm-averaged information gain bar-gamma(T). That improvement is not justified for heterogeneous kernels. These issues require corrected arguments before the stated bounds can be accepted.

The evaluation does not adequately isolate the contribution of the new scope-selection rule. Comparisons primarily involve CaBO and CoBO, whose policy restrictions already explain several performance gaps. There is no comparison with Functional Causal BO or Model-Based Causal BO where applicable, and no uniform-selection or alternative scope-selection ablation. The context and backend ablations do not resolve this attribution problem.

Scalability claims exceed the evidence. Section 3 explicitly requires exponential scope enumeration, yet the experiments involve only one or two retained POMPSs. The 86-variable example largely adds redundant variables and still has only two candidate scopes. Without enumeration timings, candidate-count scaling, or end-to-end runtime measurements, it demonstrates dimensionality reduction rather than scalable search over many scopes.

The relationship between theory and implementation is unclear. The analysis assumes known, fixed GP kernels and the specified GP-UCB procedure, while experiments use HEBO with learned transformations. The manuscript does not establish that these changes preserve the confidence or scope-selection guarantees, and it omits concrete experimental exploration-parameter settings. Although a public implementation is promised, the supplied manuscript provides no repository URL.

Experimental specifications contain consequential inconsistencies. Appendix A.1.2 omits Cancer from the PSA equation but subsequently substitutes Cancer to derive a different objective and its optimum. Appendix A.3 specifies C4 as normally distributed around itself, contradicting the stated acyclic SCM. These may be typographical errors, but they change the written environments and prevent unambiguous reproduction.
